        <a href="/new-1minute-reads/rolex-fight-against-custom-watches-comes-to-canada">Rolex’s Fight Against Custom Watches Comes to Canada</a>
      
    </h1>
    <div class="entry-info">
      <span class="published"><a href="/new-1minute-reads/rolex-fight-against-custom-watches-comes-to-canada" title="Permalink" class="permalink"><time datetime="2026-08-21">August 21, 2026</time></a></span>

    <div class="body entry-content"><div class="sqs-layout sqs-grid-12 columns-12" data-layout-label="Post Body" data-type="item" id="item-6a883fc970343c37f8231b48"><div class="row sqs-row"><div class="col sqs-col-12 span-12"><div class="sqs-block html-block sqs-block-html" data-block-type="2" data-sqsp-block="text" id="block-39862b000f363590b3d2"><div class="sqs-block-content">

<div class="sqs-html-content" data-sqsp-text-block-content>
  <p class="" data-rte-preserve-empty="true" style="white-space: pre-wrap;">Julien Duguay, founder of Quebec jeweler Bijoux Medusa, said in a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.facebook.com/BijouxMedusa/posts/pfbid02vwvjDRda88VvM9VogfmKX81mpBgfsNkvCzaKSqLWfZQzak4SfbHe361FV3Dwa4Knl">Facebook post</a> last week he will “vigorously contest” a lawsuit filed by Rolex. Rolex accuses him of selling counterfeit watches because they were modified with aftermarket diamonds and other precious stones. The case is important because it could set a precedent for Canada’s market.</p><p class="" data-rte-preserve-empty="true" style="white-space: pre-wrap;">At issue is whether a Rolex is still a Rolex if the movement and case are from the brand, but the bezel has been replaced with a diamond-studded one not made by Rolex. Courts in the U.S., Switzerland and France have generally sided with Rolex when businesses sell modified watches, while allowing customers to have their own watches personalized, a distinction <a target="_blank" href="/new-1minute-reads/customized-rolex-copyright-law">reported</a> by Coronet. In an interesting twist, a U.S. appeals court <a target="_blank" href="/new-1minute-reads/appeals-court-finds-for-rolex-watch-usa">has ruled</a> that adding diamonds to genuine dials without removing or reapplying Rolex trademarks does not constitute trademark infringement.</p><p class="" data-rte-preserve-empty="true" style="white-space: pre-wrap;">Mr. Duguay argues that Rolex is seeking to “control and dominate” the pre-owned Rolex market. He said the lawsuit, coming as Bijoux Medusa prepares to open a Montreal boutique near official Rolex retailers, is “an attempt to intimidate a local Canadian business.”</p><p class="" data-rte-preserve-empty="true" style="white-space: pre-wrap;">The lawsuit against Mr. Duguay is the latest sign Rolex is building legal precedent around the world, one case at a time, redefining what makes a counterfeit watch. Bamford, Artisans de Genève, MAD Paris, Blaken, La Californienne, as well as dealers in Texas and Georgia have faced similar pressure from the brand. Canada has little case law on the issue, making the Bijoux Medusa an important one for Rolex.</p>

CPO watches come with a two-year guarantee, requiring servicing as more are traded in. We still don’t know what watch components will be made at Rolex’s new <a href="https://www.coronet.org/new-1minute-reads/tag/Bulle+Manufacture">Bulle manufacture</a>, but we do know it will include a hub for Rolex World Service, a sign of the growing need facing the biggest luxury watch brand.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Rolex’s strategy is to push more servicing to local retailers and develop on-demand services outside the brand’s own service centers. Rolex says it has established guidelines for retailers to help speed estimates, maintenance and repairs, while promoting services such as polishing. It is launching for the first time an After-Sales Service Polisher program, a three-month course training specialists for retailer workshops, alongside its existing 18-month watchmaker program. The share of customer servicing performed by retailer watchmakers is growing, the brand says, and is reaching nearly half (49%) of all servicing operations. “The brand’s objective is to offer more local services, thereby ensuring shorter lead times through a streamlined process,” Rolex said.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Rolex also wants to streamline when parts need to be replaced, a decision usually left to the watchmaker. It keeps spare parts available in Geneva for up to 35 years after production ends and can make some parts to order for collectors’ watches. Now it plans standardized rules for replacing individual components, reducing the need for new parts. “These principles will be fully defined by 2030 for all serviced models,” Rolex said.</p>

<div class="sqs-html-content" data-sqsp-text-block-content>
  <p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">The discontinuation of the GMT-Master II "Pepsi" was not completely a surprise. What is a surprise today is that four months after the brand <a href="/new-1minute-reads/by-retiring-its-most-popular-gmt-master-ii-rolex-lets-the-myth-grow">killed off</a> one of its most difficult-to-obtain watches, prices have settled so quickly, in one of the most unusual market responses to a Rolex discontinuation.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">The model might be iconic, but today’s prices suggest there is a limit to what buyers will pay for a bezel color. With more GMT-Master II options than ever, the market is deciding just how much red and blue is worth. </p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Still, the market is skeptical the 126710BLRO is the last Pepsi. When Coronet asked a Rolex rep about the fate of one of its biggest icons, the response from Geneva seemed purposely ambiguous. So, the Pepsi’s historical importance is working <em>against</em> its premium, something we've rarely seen at Rolex. The market fears an improved version will draw buyers to the new watch, especially if Rolex has perfected the bicolor-bezel process.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">But the more interesting explanation may be long-term psychology. Few Rolex watches have been rumored for discontinuation as often as the Pepsi. As prices steadily rose in anticipation, much of the effect was already baked in, leaving little new catalyst when production finally ended. To be sure, prices did jump once the discontinuation became official, but they settled far sooner than anyone expected, as Coronet <a href="/new-1minute-reads/the-rolex-pepsi-boom-is-already-cooling" target="">observed</a> already in May. </p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Finally, there is the unusual way the Pepsi market was divided. The model was nearly impossible to get at retail, and buyers willing to pay a premium had turned to the secondary market long ago. Those who refused and stayed on retailers’ waitlists are not suddenly willing to pay premium prices today. Ending production simply closed the already-tight retail route; it did not remove the thousands of Pepsis in circulation on the preowned market, many of them hoarded by dealers who were lying in wait.</p>

<div class="sqs-html-content" data-sqsp-text-block-content>
  <p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Almost a year after Rolex invited President Donald Trump to the U.S. Open, the brand has invited another member of his administration, this time behind the doors of its manufactures in Geneva.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">On Thursday, U.S. Ambassador to Switzerland Callista Gingrich visited Rolex for the first time, touring its watchmaking facilities, learning about the history of the brand and meeting CEO Jean-Frédéric Dufour and General Counsel Alexander Troller. The meeting is the latest example of Rolex's unusually visible role in U.S.-Swiss relations <a href="https://www.coronet.org/new-1minute-reads/tag/Dufour+and+Trump">chronicled </a>by Coronet.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">It is Ms. Gingrich's first visit to a Swiss watch manufacture since becoming ambassador, after being nominated by Trump in Dec. 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in Sept. 2025. In April, she attended Watches and Wonders in Geneva, meeting several members of the industry, including Watches and Wonders Geneva Foundation CEO Matthieu Humair and Patek Philippe President Thierry Stern.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Thursday’s visit to Rolex’s headquarters comes as trade remains sensitive between Washington and Bern. Less than three weeks ago, new U.S. duties on Swiss imports took effect, generally bringing the rate to 12.5%. While Rolex regularly invites new Testimonees to tour its facilities, visits by ambassadors are rare.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Mr. Troller's presence is perhaps the most intriguing part of the visit. Rolex's first in-house general counsel joined the brand just last year, <a href="https://www.coronet.org/new-1minute-reads/rolex-appoints-in-house-counsel">as first reported</a> by Coronet, and his appearance alongside Dufour is a sign his role may reach beyond legal matters as Rolex now navigates a complex geopolitical environment. The ambassador's visit follows a year in which Mr. Dufour hosted Mr. Trump at the U.S. Open, <a href="/new-1minute-reads/rolex-letter-senator-no-tariff-talks-trump">answered questions</a> from a U.S. senator about the invitation and traveled to the Oval Office with other Swiss executives.</p>

<div class="sqs-html-content" data-sqsp-text-block-content>
  <p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Rolex has registered a name that may point to a new movement technology. A Swiss trademark application for STELLOXI published last week covers Class 14, including watches and watch components. The filing does not say what Stelloxi is.</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">Rolex’s silicon hairspring, introduced in 2014, was named "Syloxi" and is made from a composite of silicon and silicon oxide. Currently used on small- and medium-diameter Rolex models and thinner watches, the material resists magnetic fields and compensates for temperature changes. The similarity in name raises the possibility that Stelloxi could be another silicon-based hairspring, though "Stell-" (from Latin <em>stella</em>, star, perhaps?) is even further away than "Syl-" for "silicon."</p><p class="" style="white-space:pre-wrap;">A Rolex patent <a href="https://www.coronet.org/new-1minute-reads/rolex-new-mainspring-patent">previously covered by Coronet</a> but not yet used in any Rolex watch replaces the conventional hairspring with a spiral made from hundreds of repeating, linked elements designed to store more energy in the same space, allowing a watch to run longer or power more complications — a <a href="https://www.coronet.org/new-1minute-reads/can-rolex-bring-back-the-padellone">moonphase</a>, perhaps? — without a larger barrel.</p>
